senses.gloss:
siddhis
(‘powers’)
------------------------------------------
In general, the word siddhi indicates the fulfillment of any effort. In a more technical sense, it stands for the supernatural powers gained by sādhanas (yogic exercises and spiritual practices).
The Yogasūtras (4.1) of पतञ्जलि (200 B. C.) states that सिद्धिस् are attained by janma (birth), auṣadhi (drugs), मन्त्र (sacred word), तपस् (austerity) and समाधि (perfect concentration).
Eight सिद्धिस्, called अष्टसिद्धिस्, are generally mentioned by the treatises on योग like the Yogasūtras (3.45) (See AṢṬASIDDHIS for details.). This work mentions several other सिद्धिस् also (from 2.35 up to 3.48).
A warning too is administered about their being obstacles in the path, before realisation (vide 3.37).

siddhas
(‘the perfected ones’)
------------------------------------------
The word siddha has been used in several senses. Literally, it means anyone who has attained perfection.
The सिद्धस्, like the गन्धर्वस्, are a group of demigods endowed with certain miraculous powers.
Those of the human beings who have attained the अष्टसिद्धिस् (eight miraculous powers) (vide Yogasūtras 3.45), are called सिद्धस्.
Alchemists who tried to convert base metals into gold or transform the internal body-chemistry to make an old body into a young one, by the process known as kāyakalpa, were also called सिद्धस्.
Some physicians who broke away from the traditional आयुर्वेद and formed the school of Siddha System of Medicine wherein only the products of plants, roots and trees were used for preparing medicines, came to be known as सिद्धस्.
Some Tamil poets of the seventh and eighth centuries—like तिरुमूलर् and शिव-vakkiyar—who were heterodox in their attitudes and rebels against the hierarchy of the चस्ते स्य्स्तेम् were also known as the siddha(r)s.

siddhānta
(‘an established tenet’)
------------------------------------------
In the most general sense, this word means a theory. It has to be established firmly after countering effectively all the doubts and objections raised against it.
In the न्याय philosophy (vide न्याय-sūtras 1.1.26 to 31), it is classified into four types: sarvatantrasiddhānta (a dogma of all the schools); pratitantrasiddhānta (a dogma peculiar to some school); adhikaraṇasiddhānta (a hypothetical dogma) and abhyupagamasiddhānta (an implied dogma).
The example for the first dogma is that all schools accept the existence of the five elements (earth, water etc.).
‘Something can never come out of nothing.’ This dogma of the Sāṅkhya philosophy is accepted by similar schools but rejected by opposite schools. This is the example for the second सिद्धान्त.
In the third सिद्धान्त, acceptance of one fact leads to the acceptance of other facts. For instance, acceptance of the जीव or the सोउल् as the experiencer leads to the acceptance of senses and their respective objects.
In the last सिद्धान्त a tenet which is not explicitly declared as such, follows from the examination of particulars concerning it. For example, when it is discussed whether sound is eternal or non-eternal, it presupposes or implies that sound is a substance.
Special works on Hindu अस्त्रोनोम्य् and अस्त्रोलोग्य् based on the Vedāṅga ज्यौतिष are also called Siddhāntas. They are nine in number: Brahmasiddhānta; Somasiddhānta; Sūryasiddhānta; Bṛhas-patisiddhānta; Gargasiddhānta; Nārada-siddhānta; Parāśarasiddhānta; Pulastya-siddhānta; and Vasiṣṭhasiddhānta.
Obviously they are the theories put forward by these different sages.

Siddhāntabindu
------------------------------------------
For the benefit of ordinary sādhakas (seekers of spiritual wisdom), शङ्कर (A. D. 788-820) composed a few elementary treatises known as prakaraṇas which describe succinctly the essence of his Advaita Vedānta. One such work—which appears more like a स्तोत्र or a devotional hymn—is the Daśaślokī, in ten verses.
Madhusūdana सरस्वती (A. D. 1490-1580), a well-known writer of Advaita philosophy, has written a fairly long commentary on this Daśaślokī, known as the Siddhāntabindu.
Apart from countering the arguments of other schools of philosophy, this work also tries to elucidate and syncretize the various views within the Advaita philosophy itself.
It has four commentaries.

Siddhāśrama
------------------------------------------
This is the place where वामन (the fifth of the ten incarnations of विष्णु) pushed the emperor बलि to the netherworld. Again it was here that राम killed Subāhu and drove away Mārīca. In course of time it became a place of तपस् or austerities for sages like कश्यप and विश्वामित्र who established their hermitages here. It has been identified with the modern town Buxar in Uttar Pradesh.
